warmup.q: sealed interface Either<out L, out R> with data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>. In fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2>, can the Left branch simply return this?
options: No: this is an Either<L, R>, and the function must return an Either<L, R2>
Yes: a Left<L> is an Either<L, Nothing>, which is an Either<L, R2> because Nothing is a subtype of R2 and R is out
Only with an unchecked cast to Either<L, R2>
Only if R2 is the same type as R
warmup.why: After the smart cast, this is a Left<L>, whose declared supertype is Either<L, Nothing>. With out R, Nothing below R2 means Either<L, Nothing> is below Either<L, R2>. So one Left object is a valid result for any success type. Java, with no Nothing, has to build a new Left in that branch.

sections.h: Either: two out parameters and Nothing do the work
sections.html:
This lesson puts the whole track to work in four small designs. Each one uses a different tool, and the lab asks you to build all four. The first is a result type that is either a failure or a success:

Java
// Java 21: a sealed interface and records. Java has no Nothing, so Left carries an R it never uses.
sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {}
record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {}
record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {}

static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) {
    return switch (e) {
        case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value());          // must rebuild: a Left<L, R> is not a Left<L, R2>
        case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value()));
    };
}
Kotlin
sealed interface Either<out L, out R> {
    data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>
    data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R>
}

fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) {
    is Either.Left -> this                                 // no rebuild needed
    is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value))
}

Two tools from this track meet here. Either only hands values out, so both parameters are out (lesson 4). And Left fills the unused side with Nothing, the bottom type from lesson 10. Put together, a Left<String> is an Either<String, Nothing>, and because Nothing is a subtype of every type and R is out, it is also an Either<String, R2> for any R2. That's why is Either.Left -> this type-checks: the same object is a valid result for any success type. Java has neither tool, so its map must build a new Left every time.

In payment code this is the shape of validation: fun validate(auth: Authorization): Either<RejectReason, ApprovedAuthorization>. A caller can map the success, fall back with getOrElse, or when over both cases, and because Either is sealed the compiler checks that both are handled. Unlike an exception, the failure is part of the signature.

Covariance also makes results compose: an Either<String, Long> is an Either<Any, Number>, so a function that reports any failure and any numeric result accepts it. Remove the outs and almost everything breaks at once, including the Left and Right declarations themselves: Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'Either<L (of class Left<out L>), Nothing>'. A supertype is a position too.

try.title: Fold, mapLeft, then remove out
steps: Run EitherDemo and EitherDemoJava. Compare how mapLeft handles the Right branch in each.
In EitherDemo.kt, remove both outs from sealed interface Either (keep the ones on Left and Right). Predict how many lines break, then run.

code.title: EitherDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo /** Both parameters are out: an Either only hands values out. Left and Right fill the other side with Nothing. */ sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } /** Maps the failure side. `is Right -> this` type-checks because a Right<R> is an Either<Nothing, R>. */ fun <L, R, L2> Either<L, R>.mapLeft(f: (L) -> L2): Either<L2, R> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> Either.Left(f(value)) is Either.Right -> this } fun <L, R, T> Either<L, R>.fold(onLeft: (L) -> T, onRight: (R) -> T): T = when (this) { is Either.Left -> onLeft(value) is Either.Right -> onRight(value) } fun parseCents(text: String): Either<String, Long> = text.toLongOrNull()?.let { Either.Right(it) } ?: Either.Left("not a number: $text") fun main() { val ok = parseCents("1200") val bad = parseCents("12,00") println(ok.fold({ "error: $it" }, { "cents: $it" })) println(bad.mapLeft { it.uppercase() }) val wider: Either<Any, Number> = ok // out on both sides: String -> Any, Long -> Number println("wider = $wider") // Break it: remove both `out`s from `sealed interface Either` (keep them on Left and Right), // run, and read the errors in mapLeft and on the `wider` line. }

alt.title: EitherDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of EitherDemo.kt, with a sealed interface and records (Java 21 pattern matching). * Java has no Nothing, so Left must carry an R it never uses, and mapLeft must build a new Right. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, L2> Either<L2, R> mapLeft(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends L2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(f.apply(l.value())); case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(r.value()); // can't reuse r: it is an Either<L, R> }; } static <L, R, T> T fold(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends T> onLeft, Function<? super R, ? extends T> onRight) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> onLeft.apply(l.value()); case Right<L, R> r -> onRight.apply(r.value()); }; } static Either<String, Long> parseCents(String text) { try { return new Right<>(Long.parseLong(text)); } catch (NumberFormatException ex) { return new Left<>("not a number: " + text); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Either<String, Long> ok = parseCents("1200"); Either<String, Long> bad = parseCents("12,00"); System.out.println(EitherDemoJava.<String, Long, String>fold(ok, l -> "error: " + l, r -> "cents: " + r)); System.out.println(mapLeft(bad, String::toUpperCase)); Either<? extends Object, ? extends Number> wider = ok; // Java: wildcards at the use site System.out.println("wider = " + wider); } }

try.expect: Both print cents: 1200, the upper-cased failure (Left(value=NOT A NUMBER: 12,00) in Kotlin, Left[value=...] for the Java record) and wider = Right(value=1200). Kotlin's mapLeft returns this for a Right; Java builds a new Right. Without the outs you get six errors: Left and Right themselves (Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position ...), mapLeft's when, two in parseCents, and Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Either<Any, Number>', actual 'Either<String, Long>'.

sections.h: Split reading from writing: a covariant repository view
sections.html:
The second design is a repository. A full repository both takes entities (save) and returns them (findAll, findById), so it must be invariant, and an audit job that wants to read any repository can't accept a Repository<Merchant, Long> as a Repository<Entity<Long>, Long>. The fix is to split the interface by variance: put the reading half in its own covariant interface.

Java
interface ReadRepository<T> { List<T> findAll(); }               // Java: invariant, so...

static void printAll(ReadRepository<? extends Entity<?>> repo) {  // ...each reader writes ? extends
    for (Entity<?> e : repo.findAll()) System.out.println("entity " + e.getId());
}
Kotlin
interface Entity<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID }

interface ReadRepository<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }      // only hands T out

interface Repository<T : Entity<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : ReadRepository<T> {
    fun save(entity: T): T                                        // takes T in: invariant
    fun findById(id: ID): T?
}

fun printAll(repo: ReadRepository<Entity<*>>) {
    for (e in repo.findAll()) println("entity ${e.id}")
}

Now printAll accepts a Repository<Merchant, Long> and a Repository<Settlement, String>, because each one is a ReadRepository of its entity, and the read side is covariant. The full repository is still invariant, and the compiler still refuses val anyEntity: Repository<Entity<Long>, Long> = merchants with Initializer type mismatch. Nothing was weakened; the safe half was given its own name.

The bounds are lesson 2's tools: ID : Comparable<ID> lets the in-memory implementation keep entities in a TreeMap sorted by id, and T : Entity<ID> ties each entity to its id type. The Kotlin docs give the same advice for reading and writing dictionaries: split the interface instead of casting. This is interface segregation, done by variance.

Notice where the variance came from. You didn't decide that ReadRepository is covariant; you looked at its members, saw that each one only returns T, and the compiler agreed. That is the habit this track has been building: read the positions, and let them tell you.

steps: Run RepositoryDemo (or RepositoryDemoJava). One printAll reads merchants, settlements and a writable repository.
Uncomment the wrong move in each file, predict, run.

code.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo interface Entity<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID } data class Merchant(override val id: Long, val name: String) : Entity<Long> data class Settlement(override val id: String, val cents: Long) : Entity<String> /** The read side only hands T out, so it can be covariant. */ interface ReadRepository<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } /** The full repository takes a T in save, so it stays invariant. */ interface Repository<T : Entity<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : ReadRepository<T> { fun save(entity: T): T } /** An audit job that reads entities of ANY kind. */ fun printAll(repo: ReadRepository<Entity<*>>) { for (e in repo.findAll()) println(" entity ${e.id}") } fun main() { val merchants: ReadRepository<Merchant> = object : ReadRepository<Merchant> { override fun findAll() = listOf(Merchant(2, "Bakery"), Merchant(7, "Kiosk")) } val settlements: ReadRepository<Settlement> = object : ReadRepository<Settlement> { override fun findAll() = listOf(Settlement("s-1", 1_200)) } println("merchants:"); printAll(merchants) // a ReadRepository<Merchant> IS a ReadRepository<Entity<*>> println("settlements:"); printAll(settlements) val writable: Repository<Merchant, Long> = object : Repository<Merchant, Long> { override fun save(entity: Merchant) = entity override fun findAll() = listOf(Merchant(9, "Florist")) } println("writable, through its read view:"); printAll(writable) // the read side is still covariant // Wrong move. sections.h: A typed event bus: events flow out, handlers take them in
sections.html:
The third design is the one in the figure: an event bus for a payment service. Events flow out of publishers, and handlers take them in. That's lessons 4 and 5 in one class.

Java
final class Router {
    private final List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> adapters = new ArrayList<>();

    <E extends PaymentEvent> void on(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) {   // Consumer Super
        adapters.add(event -> {
            if (type.isInstance(event)) handler.accept(type.cast(event));
        });
    }
}
Kotlin
class EventBus {
    private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<out PaymentEvent>, MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>>()

    fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) {
        handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }
            .add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }      // the adapter
    }

    fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) { handlers[event::class]?.forEach { it(event) } }
}

Every piece has a reason. The map's keys are KClass<out PaymentEvent>, because that's the type of event::class (lesson 9). The handler can't go into the list as it is, and the compiler explains why: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(E (of fun <E : PaymentEvent> on)) -> Unit', but '(PaymentEvent) -> Unit' was expected. A function that only takes CardAuthorized can't be handed a RefundIssued; function parameters are in. So the bus stores an adapter that takes any PaymentEvent, checks it with safeCast, and passes on only an E. The same in works in your favor at the call site: an audit handler of type (PaymentEvent) -> Unit can subscribe under CardAuthorized::class.

For Kotlin callers, add the reified wrapper from lesson 8, with one new word:

Java
// Java callers pass the class: bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraudCheck(e));
// There is no Java equivalent of the reified, noinline wrapper.
Kotlin
inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(noinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = subscribe(E::class, handler)

bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraudCheck(it) }

A lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, which means it doesn't exist as an object. This one gets stored in the map, so it has to stay an object: noinline says so.

One limit to know: this bus routes by the exact class. A handler subscribed under PaymentEvent::class never runs, because no event's run-time class is the interface itself. The "Go deeper" part shows how to walk supertypes when you need that.

sections.h: Typed keys: one map, many value types, no casts at the call site
sections.html:
The last design is a container for values of many types, the kind of per-payment context a Quarkus request or a Temporal workflow carries around: the accepted currencies, the retry delays, the retry count. Lesson 9's registry used the type as the whole key. Here the key is a small object that carries a name and the full type of its value:

Java
record Key<T>(String name, Type type) {                       // Type from a super type token
    static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); }
}
static final Key<List<String>> CURRENCIES = Key.of("currencies", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {});

<T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); }
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
<T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); }        // safe: only set puts values in
Kotlin
data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType)
inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>())

val CURRENCIES = key<List<String>>("currencies")

operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value }
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T?   // safe: only set puts values in

val currencies: List<String>? = attributes[CURRENCIES]       // no cast, no type argument at the call site

The key's type parameter does the typing: attributes[CURRENCIES] is a List<String>? with no cast at the call site, and attributes[CURRENCIES] = 42 is a compile error (Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected.). The KType inside the key makes key<List<Long>>("retries") and key<Int>("retries") different keys, so two teams can't collide by picking the same name.

Key<T> is invariant on purpose, and this is the last variance decision of the track. Declare it out T, and a Key<List<String>> becomes a Key<Any>. Then attributes[currencies] = 42 compiles, with T inferred as Any, and the next read of the currencies throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List. A key is used to write as well as to read, so it can't be a producer. The one unchecked cast in get stays safe only as long as that holds.

This is also a good place to stop adding generics. Four designs, two commented casts, one deliberately invariant key: if a design needs much more than that, a plainer one with a sealed class and a when is usually easier for the next engineer to read.

try.title: Store typed attributes, then break the key
steps: Run TypedKeysDemo and TypedKeysDemoJava. Neither call site has a cast.
Read LeakyKey in the Kotlin file: the same key with out T. Find the line where the bad value goes in, and the line where it fails.
Uncomment the wrong move in each file. The invariant key stops at compile time what the leaky key let through.

code.title: TypedKeysDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** Invariant on purpose: a Key<List<String>> is not a Key<Any>. */ data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class Attributes { private val values = HashMap<Key<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } /** The same thing with `out T`: it compiles, and it is broken. */ data class LeakyKey<out T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> leakyKey(name: String) = LeakyKey<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class LeakyAttributes { private val values = HashMap<LeakyKey<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: LeakyKey<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: LeakyKey<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } val CURRENCIES = key<List<String>>("currencies") val RETRIES = key<Int>("retries") fun main() { val attrs = Attributes() attrs[CURRENCIES] = listOf("EUR", "USD") attrs[RETRIES] = 3 val currencies: List<String>? = attrs[CURRENCIES] // typed by the key: no cast here println("currencies = $currencies, retries = ${attrs[RETRIES]}") val leaky = LeakyAttributes() val leakyCurrencies = leakyKey<List<String>>("currencies") leaky[leakyCurrencies] = 42 // compiles: T is inferred as Any try { val first: String? = leaky[leakyCurrencies]?.first() println(first) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs[CURRENCIES] = 42 }

alt.title: TypedKeysDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypedKeysDemo.kt. The key's type comes from a super type token; Java generics are invariant. */ public class TypedKeysDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final class Attributes { private final Map<Key<?>, Object> values = new HashMap<>(); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } } static final Key<List<String>> CURRENCIES = Key.of("currencies", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); static final Key<Integer> RETRIES = Key.of("retries", new TypeRef<Integer>() {}); public static void main(String[] args) { Attributes attrs = new Attributes(); attrs.set(CURRENCIES, List.of("EUR", "USD")); attrs.set(RETRIES, 3); List<String> currencies = attrs.get(CURRENCIES); // typed by the key: no cast here System.out.println("currencies = " + currencies + ", retries = " + attrs.get(RETRIES)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs.set(CURRENCIES, 42); } }

try.expect: Both print currencies = [EUR, USD], retries = 3. Kotlin then prints ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List: leaky[leakyCurrencies] = 42 compiled because out T let T be inferred as Any, and the read failed later. The wrong move fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. in Kotlin and method set in class Attributes cannot be applied to given types in Java.

analogy: The event bus is a post office sorting room. Letters (events) come in from every counter, which is the producing side. Each pigeonhole is labeled with a letter class, such as "registered", and each pigeonhole has clerks assigned to it, which is the consuming side. A clerk trained to handle any letter can be assigned to the registered pigeonhole: that's the (PaymentEvent) -> Unit handler under CardAuthorized::class. A clerk who only handles registered letters can't be given the general pile, so the office puts a checker in front of him who passes on only registered mail: that's the safeCast adapter. The analogy breaks at the checker. A real clerk would notice a wrong letter himself, but a Kotlin lambda can't: if you skip the adapter and cast the handler instead, the wrong event reaches it and fails with a ClassCastException inside the handler.
world: These four shapes map straight onto a payment service. A Kafka consumer decodes each record and publishes it on an in-process bus, where the fraud check, the ledger writer and the audit log subscribe by event class, and the audit log takes every PaymentEvent. Validation of an incoming authorization returns Either<RejectReason, AuthorizedPayment> instead of throwing, so a Temporal workflow can branch on it without catching exceptions across the activity boundary. A reporting job that reads merchants and settlements from Oracle takes ReadRepository<Entity<*>>, while only the write path sees the invariant Repository. And per-request context in a Quarkus endpoint (the merchant id, the accepted currencies, the idempotency key) fits a typed-key container, so context[IDEMPOTENCY_KEY] comes back as a String with no cast.
mistake: The common mistake in an event bus is casting the handler instead of wrapping it: handlers.add(handler as (PaymentEvent) -> Unit) under @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). It compiles, and every test that publishes the right event type passes. The first time an event of another class reaches that list, through a shared key, a supertype subscription or a bug in the routing, the handler receives it and throws ClassCastException: class RefundIssued cannot be cast to class CardAuthorized from inside its own body, far from the subscription that caused it. People write the cast because the adapter looks like extra ceremony, and because erasure makes the cast itself succeed. The fix is the adapter, { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }, which costs one line and makes the wrong event a no-op.

compare.title: The typed event bus in Java and Kotlin

java.title: EventBus.java
java.html: import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<? extends PaymentEvent>, List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>>> handlers = new HashMap<>(); // Consumer<? super E>: a handler for E or for any supertype of E <E extends PaymentEvent> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(event -> { if (type.isInstance(event)) handler.accept(type.cast(event)); // the adapter }); } int publish(PaymentEvent event) { List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> list = handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of()); list.forEach(h -> h.accept(event)); return list.size(); } } // bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraudCheck(e));

kotlin.title: EventBus.kt
kotlin.html: class EventBus { private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<out PaymentEvent>, MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>>() // (E) -> Unit is already Function1<in E, ...>: a handler for any supertype of E fits fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) } // the adapter } inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(noinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: PaymentEvent): Int { val list = handlers[event::class] ?: return 0 for (h in list) h(event) return list.size } } // bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraudCheck(it) }

compare.note: The design is the same in both languages: keys from the event's run-time class, handlers stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a handler parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (Class<? extends PaymentEvent> keys, Consumer<? super E> handlers), Kotlin gets it from declarations: event::class is already a KClass<out PaymentEvent>, and a function type is already in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs noinline because the lambda is stored. Java callers can use the KClass version only through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(CardAuthorized.class), so a bus meant for Java code should also offer a Class<E> overload.

worked.title: Route a card-issuer webhook through all four designs

steps.say: A webhook body arrives. 1. Parse it into an Either instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad body means.
steps.code: fun parseWebhook(body: Map<*, *>): Either<String, PaymentEvent> { val id = body["id"] as? String ?: return Either.Left("missing id") val cents = (body["cents"] as? Number)?.toLong() ?: return Either.Left("missing cents") return when (body["type"]) { "auth" -> Either.Right(CardAuthorized(id, cents)) "refund" -> Either.Right(RefundIssued(id, cents)) else -> Either.Left("unknown type ${body["type"]}") } }

alt.html: static Either<String, PaymentEvent> parseWebhook(Map<?, ?> body) { if (!(body.get("id") instanceof String id)) return new Left<>("missing id"); if (!(body.get("cents") instanceof Number n)) return new Left<>("missing cents"); long cents = n.longValue(); Object type = body.get("type"); if ("auth".equals(type)) return new Right<>(new CardAuthorized(id, cents)); if ("refund".equals(type)) return new Right<>(new RefundIssued(id, cents)); return new Left<>("unknown type " + type); }

steps.say: 1. Publish the successes on the bus. 3. Record the failures in the request's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can Either.Right(CardAuthorized(...)) be returned where Either<String, PaymentEvent> is expected? (Right<CardAuthorized> is an Either<Nothing, CardAuthorized>, and both parameters are out.)
steps.code: val LAST_ERROR = key<String>("webhook.lastError") fun handle(body: Map<*, *>, bus: EventBus, context: Attributes): Int = when (val parsed = parseWebhook(body)) { is Either.Right -> bus.publish(parsed.value) // events flow out to the handlers is Either.Left -> { context[LAST_ERROR] = parsed.value; 0 } }

alt.html: static final Key<String> LAST_ERROR = Key.of("webhook.lastError", new TypeRef<String>() {}); static int handle(Map<?, ?> body, EventBus bus, Attributes context) { return switch (parseWebhook(body)) { case Right<String, PaymentEvent> r -> bus.publish(r.value()); case Left<String, PaymentEvent> l -> { context.set(LAST_ERROR, l.value()); yield 0; } }; }

steps.say: 1. Wire the handlers once, at startup. The audit log is a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit and subscribes under both event classes; the fraud check only understands card authorizations. A nightly report reads merchants through the covariant ReadRepository<Entity<*>> view. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: safeCast in the bus adapter and the unchecked cast inside Attributes.get.
steps.code: val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { audit.write(it.paymentId) } bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized::class, auditAll) bus.subscribe(RefundIssued::class, auditAll) bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraud.check(it.paymentId, it.cents) } handle(mapOf("id" to "pay_1", "cents" to 1_200, "type" to "auth"), bus, context) // 2 handlers ran handle(mapOf("id" to "pay_2"), bus, context) // context[LAST_ERROR] == "missing cents"

alt.html: Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> audit.write(e.getPaymentId()); bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, auditAll); bus.subscribe(RefundIssued.class, auditAll); bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraud.check(e.getPaymentId(), e.getCents())); handle(Map.of("id", "pay_1", "cents", 1_200, "type", "auth"), bus, context); // 2 handlers ran handle(Map.of("id", "pay_2"), bus, context); // LAST_ERROR is "missing cents"

lab.title: Build Either, a repository, an event bus and typed keys
steps: Run the tests. All thirteen fail. Work through the files in order; each part has its own tests.
Either.kt (TODO in two functions): write map with is Either.Left -> this, and getOrElse.
Repository.kt (TODOs 1 to 3): add out to ReadRepository. Back InMemoryRepository with a java.util.TreeMap<ID, T>. Write saveAll and describeAll.

EventBus.kt (TODOs 4 to 6): store an adapter in subscribe, make the one-argument subscribe inline with reified E and a noinline handler, and write publish so it returns the number of handlers that ran.

Attributes.kt (TODOs 7 and 8): make key inline and reified with typeOf<T>(), then write set, get, getOrDefault and remove. Use key in values for getOrDefault, so a stored null is not mistaken for a missing key.
Run until all thirteen pass. Then remove out from ReadRepository once more and watch which test turns red.
hints: TreeMap works as byId[entity.id] = entity, and byId.values.toList() is already in id order.
The adapter is handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }.add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }. safeCast needs import kotlin.reflect.safeCast.
publish: val list = handlers[event::class] ?: return 0, then call each and return list.size.
Each unchecked cast in Attributes needs @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). Write one comment saying why it's safe: only set(key: Key<T>, value: T) puts values in, and Key is invariant.

drill.title: Write Either and map from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Either with Left and Right in Kotlin, with the variance and the Nothing that let map return this for a Left. Write map. Then write the Java version with a sealed interface and records, and point at the line where Java has to build a new object.

answer.html: sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> this // Either<L, Nothing> is an Either<L, R2> is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value)) }

alt.title: Either.java
alt.html: sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value()); // here: no Nothing, so a new Left case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value())); }; }

recap: Either<out L, out R> with Left : Either<L, Nothing> lets one Left stand for every success type, so map can return this. Java must rebuild it.
When a type both reads and writes T, split out the reading half as an out T interface. Readers get covariance; the full type stays invariant and safe.
In an event bus, events are produced and handlers consume. Keys are KClass<out PaymentEvent> from event::class, and handlers are stored behind a safeCast adapter.
A reified wrapper that stores its lambda needs noinline.
A typed key carries its value type (Key<T> with a KType inside), so reads need no cast and same-named keys of different types don't collide.
A key is used to write, so it must be invariant. With out T, a wrong value goes in and fails later as a ClassCastException.

explain.prompt: A teammate reviews the lab's EventBus and asks two things: why the bus wraps every handler in a lambda instead of storing it directly, and why the audit handler, typed (PaymentEvent) -> Unit, can subscribe under CardAuthorized::class. Explain both with the producer and consumer picture.
explain.answer: Events are produced by publishers and consumed by handlers, so a handler's type is in on its parameter. That gives both answers. A handler typed (CardAuthorized) -> Unit can only consume card authorizations, so it is not a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit, which must consume any event. The bus keeps one list of (PaymentEvent) -> Unit per class, so it can't store the card handler as it is. It stores an adapter instead: a function that takes any PaymentEvent, checks it with CardAuthorized::class.safeCast, and passes it on only if it really is a card authorization. Casting the handler would compile but fail with a ClassCastException inside the handler the first time a wrong event arrived. The audit handler goes the other way. It consumes every PaymentEvent, so it can certainly consume card authorizations: because the parameter is in, a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit is a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit, and subscribe(CardAuthorized::class, auditAll) type-checks with E = CardAuthorized.

deeper.html:
Each design has a natural next step.

The bus delivers only to the event's exact class. To deliver a CardAuthorized to handlers subscribed under PaymentEvent::class too, publish must walk the event's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: event.javaClass.interfaces and event.javaClass.superclass, converted with .kotlin. With kotlin-reflect, KClass.allSuperclasses lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time.

Either gets more useful with flatMap, which chains steps that can each fail: fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>. Its Left branch returns this for the same reason map can. The standard library's own Result<out T> is also declared out, but its failure side is always a Throwable; Either lets the failure be a domain type such as RejectReason. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full Either.

The repository can grow a write-only view too: interface WriteRepository<in T> { fun save(entity: T) }. A loader that writes Merchants can then accept a WriteRepository<Entity<Long>>. With both views, the invariant Repository is simply the type that is both.

The typed keys can carry a default: class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T), with get returning T instead of T?. Keep Key invariant when you do: default is read, but set still writes through the key.
